title: The classic textbook explanation of how wings lift is wrong
body: A popular explanation says air over a wing’s curved top has farther to go, so it must speed up to meet the air passing underneath, and faster air means lower pressure. The conclusion is right but the reasoning is false: nothing makes the two streams meet, and the air over the top actually moves **much faster** than that story predicts, reaching the trailing edge first. Lift comes from the wing turning the airflow downward, which pushes the wing up by Newton’s third law, and equivalently from pressure being lower above the wing than below. Each view is correct but incomplete on its own; a full account needs both.

slides.alt: A wing cross-section with one streamline passing over it and one under it. A marked parcel of air on the upper streamline is far ahead of the parcel on the lower one. An arrow behind the wing shows the flow turned downward and an arrow above the wing points up, labelled lift.
slides.caption: Two parcels of air split at the wing’s front edge. The upper one wins the race to the back, and the air leaves heading down.

left.label: Textbook myth
left.text: Air parted at the nose must meet again at the tail, so the top stream hurries and its pressure drops.

right.label: What happens
right.text: The top stream arrives well before the bottom one. Lift comes from turning the flow downward and from the pressure difference that goes with it.

slides.heading: Two right answers
slides.text: Explaining lift by flow deflection and Newton’s laws is correct but incomplete, and so is explaining it by pressure differences alone. Bernoulli’s principle is not wrong; the simple stories built on it are. A fuller explanation needs both deflection and pressure.

slides.heading: Flat wings, upside down
slides.text: A flat plate at an angle makes lift, though less than a streamlined airfoil. And a cambered wing can be flown inverted if its angle to the oncoming air is adjusted, which is how aerobatic planes fly upside down.

slides.question: What does the ‘equal transit time’ story get wrong?
options: Air over the top arrives first
Air under the wing goes faster
slides.explanation: Nothing forces the two streams to meet at the trailing edge. The air over the top of a lifting wing moves much faster than equal transit time predicts.

slides.heading: Myth or fact?

items.text: Air split at the nose must meet again at the tail
Air over the top reaches the tail first
A flat plate at an angle makes lift
A cambered wing can fly upside down

slides.explanation: Lift comes from turning the flow downward and from lower pressure above the wing; both views are right, the equal-transit story is not.
